title: Jon Speelman: Miniatures in Samarkand
summary:
The massacre of the innocents

[Note that Jon Speelman also looks at the content of the article in video format , here embedded at the end of the article.]

The Samarkand Olympiad was the largest ever with over 200 teams in the open section and only a few dozen fewer in the parallel Women's Olympiad. Consequently, there were about 800 games a day and so getting on for 9,000 overall.

Many of the best games have already been highlighted here, and I thought that I'd look for some miniatures - games of 25 moves or fewer. To restrict these to a manageable number, I took decisive games in the open section only and required at least one player to be rated over 2500. This yielded 40 games about half of which were from the "massacre of the innocents" in the first round (with pairings of top half v. bottom). I selected the best and/or most amusing with fairly light annotations and have kept them in broad chronological order.

Several oil-on-oak-panel versions of "The Massacre of the Innocents" were painted by Netherlandish painters Pieter Bruegel the Elder and his son Pieter Brueghel the Younger (c.1565-1567). The work translates the Biblical account of the Massacre of the Innocents into a scene in the Southern Netherlands in the prelude to the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule

I ended up with a "cricket team" of games, and you can find another (only slightly gratuitous) mention of cricket in the notes to game 7, Rapport v. Demchenko.

After the fiasco last month, I did finally manage to log on to XSplit via Twitch. So I've also done the usual video version this time, which I'm recording (in the regrettable absence of a time machine) on Friday, October 2 nd - my 70 th birthday .

title: From the Olympiad to the Mediterranean: Titled stars head to the Sahel Chess Festival
summary:
Chess, sea and sun

For more than a month, the global chess community was gripped by the intense battles of the FIDE Chess Olympiad and the political drama surrounding the FIDE Presidential election. Now, as the dust slowly settles, the broader chess landscape is regaining its rightful spotlight.

Privately run open tournaments remain the lifeblood of the sport, offering a crucial gateway to new heights for ambitious, hardworking players who are locked out of the exclusive elite circuits. Even when the prize funds are modest, the opportunity to secure ever-important title norms counts for a lot. When a venue perfectly fits the motto "chess, sea and sun", it adds a wonderful layer to the competitive experience. And if that tournament takes place in Africa, a continent boasting a vibrant chess community but historically lacking international open events, the picture is complete.

The Sahel Chess Festival encompasses all of these elements. From October 24 to November 1, 2026, the famous resort town of Monastir on the central Tunisian coast will host an expected 300 international competitors at the four-star Hotel El Habib. The full technical regulations and official entry details can be found on the festival's official website .

Negotiations with titled players are still ongoing, but a formidable lineup has already been confirmed. Most of them will be travelling to Monastir after only a brief respite following their gruelling schedules at the Olympiad.

Among the headliners in Group A are:

GM Titas Stremavicius (2558) of Lithuania. The national champion in 2021, 2025, and 2026, Titas has represented his country at three Chess Olympiads (2018, 2022, and 2026). At the recent Olympiad, he played on board one with an unbeaten performance, securing draws against much higher rated opponents including GM M. Amin Tabatabaei (2737, IRI), GM Nikita Vitiugov (2666, ENG), GM Alexey Sarana (2666, SRB), GM Bogdan-Daniel Deac (2644, ROU), GM Thai Dai Van Nguyen (2633, CZE) and GM Ivan Saric (2623, CRO). A qualifier for the 2025 World Cup, Titas is no stranger to upsets, having famously knocked out Wesley So in the second round.

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

GM Pavel Ponkratov (2540, FID), a dynamic Russian grandmaster who won the Russian Rapid Cup in 2017 and 2018. In 2021, he won the Russian Championship Higher League and qualified for both the Russian Superfinal and the FIDE World Cup.

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

Dutch GM Nijboer Friso (2441), represented his country in six Chess Olympiads (1996–2006). He has written four different volumes on opening theory, Tactics in the Chess Opening.

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

Representing the host nation is Tunisia's top active player, IM Kamel Njili (2406). A dedicated coach, Njili captained the Tunisian women’s team at the latest Olympiad. He recently launched the Njili Chess Academy in the capital city of Tunis, which is already training hundreds of aspiring young talents.

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

Also flying the Tunisian flag is GM Amir Zaibi (2343), who secured his grandmaster title in 2020 after winning the Arab Chess Championship.

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

GM Mihail Marin (2413) of Romania, a renowned ChessBase author , trainer and captain of the Italian women's squad at the recent Olympiad will be accompanied by his partner, the talented artist and player WFM Maria Yugina (2052, ROU).

Maria Yugina and Mihail Marin | Photo: Maria Yugina's Facebook

Two bright young prospects will enter the fray from India: WGM Priyanka Nutakki (2261) and twelve-year-old CM Aryan Mehta (2203).

Image: Sahel Chess Festival

Fully dedicated to his budding chess career, Aryan has spent the last couple of years intensively studying the game and competing internationally. In Monastir, he will be travelling with his coach, GM Farrukh Amonatov (2598) of Tajikistan.

Aryan Mehta | Photo: Sunway Sitges Chess Festival

We previewed this event several months ago . This announcement serves as a final reminder for last-minute, efficient players looking to treat themselves to a valuable Mediterranean chess experience. If you cannot make it this autumn, make sure to pencil the festival into your calendar for next year. The 2027 edition is set to move to Sousse to celebrate the historic 60 th anniversary of the legendary 1967 Sousse Interzonal, a tournament famously graced by the presence of Bobby Fischer.

title: Evren Ucok and the case for chess in developing young minds
summary:
Curing the attention crisis

By Selim Gurcan

The 2006 comedy Idiocracy paints a terrifyingly funny vision of the future. After sleeping for 500 years, an average man wakes up in a world where humanity has lost all critical thinking. People water their crops with sports drinks because commercials told them "it has electrolytes". Entertainment is reduced to mindless TV, and society is close to collapsing.

For Evren Ucok, a successful entrepreneur and chess supporter, the film reads like a warning label. With children hooked on 15-second TikTok reels and AI algorithms making every decision for them, Evren fears that logical intelligence - the most important type of intelligence, including the capacity to reason, learn and adapt - is degrading, as evidenced by the most recent PISA scores across the Western world, heavily discussed in the 8 September 2026 edition of The Economist.

Evren believes that chess is one of the best cures for the attention crisis gripping today's youth, so many of whom are trapped in the dopamine loop of short videos. Where fast-paced reels train young minds to demand instant dopamine without thinking, chess does the opposite: it forces players to calculate, evaluate and ask "why?" before committing to a move. It replaces passive scrolling with deep, focused concentration. Evren estimates that playing around 50 to 100 hours of competitive chess (even between classmates) meaningfully improves concentration ability, humility and logical reasoning in children and pre-teens, and that the effect is permanent.

An average citizen in a dystopian world 500 years from now

Backed by real commitment

That conviction is not just talk. Over the past three years, Evren has spent over $5 million on various chess causes. In particular, he supports some of the most promising young players in the world with help from renowned GMs and super-GMs who provide regular coaching.

The programme goes far beyond coaching and tournament expenses and includes career and tournament advice, chess camps, sports psychology, tailored nutrition, physical fitness and selective family stipends when necessary.

Evren also backs the Marseille Chess Club (focused on top young talents in France and underprivileged children in Marseille), the European Chess Union (focused on women's and seniors' chess), the Monte Carlo Chess Club (which won the European Women's Cup several times), and the Istanbul Chess Club, where Evren cut his teeth as a young teenager.

He is also funding advanced technology, for example chess super-engines that can calculate 500 million moves per second, and a professional chess platform for serious players that provides advanced features, encourages social play within and between offline clubs and prevents bad behaviour (cheating, stalling and trolling). His team also researched micro-devices used in OTB cheating and alerted the relevant FIDE, ECU and national authorities and tournament organisers.

The whole programme started with a single talent: GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, a Turkish prodigy who was on the brink of quitting chess for lack of support in August 2023, before he and his family met Evren through Selim Gurcan (FM, chess author and a close friend of Evren since their early teenage years around 35–40 years ago). Evren agreed to support Yagiz for at least five years and “do whatever it takes” for him to realise his full potential. Selim's close friend GM Mert Erdogdu agreed to coach Yagiz intensively. With their combined help, Yagiz went from zero GM norms to three GM norms in three consecutive tournaments, and the GM title followed soon after in April 2024.

Yagiz, Mert and Evren at Selim's house in December 2023 | Photo: Courtesy of Selim Gurcan

As Yagiz got stronger and stronger, Mert passed the flag to Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, former world No. 2 and also a long-term friend of Selim. The team also organised several training camps with top GMs and three different matches (titled Clash of Generations) for Yagiz to play and train against super-GM opponents. In these matches, Yagiz scored 12.5 points in 18 games and gained valuable experience in elite-level chess. This performance also helped him cross 2700 Elo (super-GM level) at the age of 14, the youngest in history. Now 15, Yagiz is the world's No. 1 junior (under 20).

The success of Yagiz encouraged Evren and Selim to support more prodigies, including Ediz Gurel and Isik Can, who, together with Yagiz, make up the top three in Turkiye by Elo, as well as the Turkish national team.

Gaining confidence from the programme's success, they soon began supporting top talents from other countries too.

Clash of Generations: Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus v. Peter Svidler (eight-time Russian champion) | Photo: Marseille Chess Club

Luca Protopopescu (age 10)

They started with Luca Protopopescu, a young talent from Marseille discovered by GM Mert Erdogdu, a close friend of Selim who had coached Yagiz when he was younger. With Mert’s help, Luca became the youngest person in history to cross 2200 Elo - the rating level separating top amateurs from real professionals - at the age of 9 years and 5 days. A long and highly personalised congratulatory letter soon followed from President Emmanuel Macron of France.

Luca with his cup and reading Asterix after the French Championship in May 2025 | Photo: Courtesy of Selim Gurcan

Bodhana Sivanandan (age 11)

Evren started supporting Bodhana in January 2026 after he and Bodhana's father, Sivanandan Velayutham, were introduced by UK chess legend Malcolm Pein (and soon became friends). Already a rising star, Bodhana soon became the youngest girl in history to defeat a 2600+ rated GM, breaking a record held since 1988 by chess legend Judit Polgar, who is widely considered to be the strongest woman chess player in history and featured in the popular Netflix documentary “Queen of Chess”. A couple of weeks after this success and an ambitious chess camp in Marseille organised by her coach, GM Mert Erdogdu, she became the youngest British Women’s Champion in history at the age of 11.

Bodhana Sivanandan as British Women's Champion | Photo: Yury Krylov

Marc Llari (age 13)

Marc is no stranger to success. In June 2026, after working for 10 months with Mert, he won the U12 (under-12) World Cup with an impressive score of 9/11 and finished the event undefeated. The Marseille-trained prodigy also won his first IM norm at the Spilimbergo Masters tournament in Italy in August 2026, scoring 5.5/9 with draws against GM Jan Šubelj (2549) and GM Kirk Ghazarian (2535), for a 2456 performance rating.

Marc as U12 World Champion in June 2026 | Photo: FIDE

Christian Glöckler (age 14)

Evren started supporting Christian in March 2026 after hearing about the impressive talent from IM Stefan Löffler. Shortly afterwards, the German IM won the Masters Open at the renowned 59th Biel International Chess Festival in July 2026 with a round to spare, scoring 8/10 with a 2597 performance and clinching his first grandmaster norm, sealed by a ninth-round win over GM Dimitris Alexakis. Already rated above 2500, he now needs two more norms for the GM title.

Christian won the 2026 Tata Steel Qualifiers with a remarkable 8½/9 | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Atilla Kuru (age 15)

Evren and Selim started supporting Atilla in December 2024 after meeting him and his parents through Turkish GM Dragan Solak. After his first GM norm at the 2024 European Individual Championship, Atilla took his second norm at the Sardinia World Chess Festival in May 2026. Days later, he finished second at the Young Talents GM Norm tournament in Stockholm. With his score of 6.5/9, he won 13 rating points and passed the critical threshold of 2500 Elo. Shortly afterwards, at the 27th Sants Barcelona Open in August 2026, he secured his third and final GM norm. He finished the ten-round event unbeaten with a 2656 performance, taking his rating past 2520 and making him Turkiye's latest grandmaster at 15.

Atilla, Marc and Luca, with Mert and Selim | Photo: Courtesy of Selim Gurcan

Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus (age 15)

In August 2026, just after turning 15, Yagiz became the world's highest-rated junior (under 20) as well as the youngest person in history (by a wide margin) to exceed 2700 Elo.

At the recent 2026 Chess Olympiad, Yagiz was first board for Turkiye, playing against many top super-GMs, including Abdusattorov, Caruana and Keymer. Despite the difficult field, he scored 8/10 (6 wins, 4 draws) with a 2839 performance, which earned him the silver medal on board 1. He also gained 15 Elo points, increasing his live Elo to 2731 (No. 17 globally).

Live rating list after the 2026 Olympiad

Aydin Suleymanli (age 21)

Azerbaijani talent Aydin Suleymanli showed steady improvement last year. He recently defeated Uzbek rising star Mukhiddin Madaminov 4.5–1.5 in a six-game match, pushing his rating above 2670 for the first time and placing him firmly in the top 50 of chess at No. 45. Coached by the legendary Rustam Kasimcanov, the first world chess champion from Uzbekistan (another Turkic country), as well as by Shakhriyar from his home country, the young Turk is now playing board two for his country at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand (behind Shakhriyar) and working towards reaching 2700 Elo.

Rustam and Aydin after Aydin's surprising victory over chess GOAT Magnus Carlsen in the World Team Rapid and Blitz Championship in June 2026 | Photo: Michal Walusza

Isik Can (age 21)

The oldest member of the prodigy group, GM Isik Can won the 2026 Liaocheng Rising Stars tournament in China without losing a game, defeating 2618-rated GM Aleksey Grebnev along the way. The 2025 Turkish Champion also led the University of Missouri to the US National Collegiate title. Studying business at the University of Missouri, Isik earned his GM title during his first semester, showing that academic and elite chess ambitions can go hand in hand. At the time this article is being written, Isik is playing board three for Turkiye in the 2026 Olympiad.

2025 Turkish champion Isik Can with his cup | Photo: Turkish Chess Federation

Clash of prodigies

The top two of these prodigies, Aydin Suleymanli and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, found themselves competing head-to-head at the Biel Masters Triathlon. Aydin finished second in the Biel Masters Triathlon and Yagiz Kaan third, behind only the experienced elite player Levon Aronian. Aydin had stepped in at short notice, and Yagiz posted the second-best result of the blitz phase - more evidence of the fearless, attacking chess that lit up his Tata Steel Masters run earlier in the year.

Aydin and Yagiz playing at the Biel Masters Triathlon | Photo: Biel Chess Festival

Marseille chess camp and Cannes family gathering

These impressive results are only part of the story. Beyond teaching concentration and humility and improving logical reasoning, chess also brings people together, and it builds lasting bonds between players, coaches and families, as two recent gatherings in the South of France showed.

At the training camp between 13 and 18 July hosted by Marseille-Echecs, which is headed by Laurie Delorme and William Azari, GM Mert Erdogdu and GM Pierre Laurent-Paoli trained with prodigies Bodhana Sivanandan, Marc Llari, Luca Protopopescu and Joachim Le Geay. The reigning European Women's Champion, 15-year-old Anastasiia Hnatyshyn (whom Evren met through his Ukrainian friend IM Igor Berezovsky), joined the camp as a guest for a few days. The camp turned out to be remarkably productive, and impressive results followed shortly afterwards. Bodhana and Marc earned their first IM norms after a few weeks. Anastasiia now leads the strong Ukrainian women's team at the 2026 Chess Olympiad.

Anastasiia, Bodhana, Marc, Luca and Joachim with GM Laurent-Paoli | Photo: Courtesy of Selim Gurcan

title: Main decisions of the FIDE General Assembly 2026
summary:
Press release by FIDE

The FIDE General Assembly was held on 26–27 September 2026 in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, during the 46 th FIDE Chess Olympiad and the FIDE Congress 2026. The Congress brought together representatives of FIDE Member Federations, as well as members of the FIDE Council, Zonal Council and FIDE Commissions. The General Assembly agenda included elections, reports and financial matters, membership issues, administrative matters, changes to the FIDE Handbook, the FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030, and other matters.

Elections and appointments

The General Assembly took the following decisions concerning the FIDE leadership and commissions:

Mr. Timur Turlov was elected FIDE President.

Mr. Viswanathan Anand was elected FIDE Deputy President.

The following were elected by the General Assembly as FIDE Vice-Presidents:

Ms. Yuhua Xu (CHN)

Mr. Michael Khodarkovsky (USA)

Mr. Pavel Kolobkov (RUS)

Mr. Yassin Souleiman Hassan (DJI)

The following nominees of the FIDE President were elected:

Mr. Luigi Maggi (ITA) – Treasurer

Ms. Bouchra Kadiri (MAR) – Vice-President/Secretary of the FIDE Council

Mr. Mahir Mammedov (AZE) – Vice-President

Ms. Carol S. Williams Pesqueira (ARU) – Vice-President

Mr. Mykhailo Podolyak (UKR) – Vice-President

The following nominees of the FIDE President as Honorary Vice-Presidents of FIDE were proposed for approval by the FIDE Council:

Mr. Rustam Kasimdzhanov (UZB)

Mr. Javier Ochoa De Echaguen (ESP)

Mr. Fouad Fahmi Darwish (UAE)

Mr. Michael Stoettinger (AUT)

The General Assembly also:

Elected Mr. Francois Strydom (RSA) as a Member of the Constitutional Commission.

Supported President's decision to appoint Mr. Jorge Arias (URU) as Secretary of the Constitutional Commission.

Changes to the FIDE Charter and Regulations

The General Assembly considered a number of proposals concerning the FIDE Charter and regulations. Appointing the Honorary Vice-Presidents of FIDE The General Assembly approved the proposal of the FIDE President, to appoint up to 5 Honorary Vice-Presidents entitled to participate in the work of the Council with all rights, except for voting rights. The list of proposed nominees is mentioned above.

Bilingual institutional designation

The General Assembly approved an amendment to the FIDE Charter concerning the bilingual institutional designation of FIDE, recognising the historical French name of the organisation alongside its English designation. Under the new Article 5.7, whenever FIDE displays its full institutional name together with the FIDE acronym, seal, flag or emblem, the English and French names will be presented jointly as: International Chess Federation / Fédération Internationale des Échecs. The amendment concerns FIDE's institutional identity and visual representation only. It does not change the status of English as FIDE's official and working language and does not introduce a general requirement to translate FIDE documents, regulations, decisions, minutes, contracts, correspondence, news or other communications into French.

Chess960 rating

The General Assembly approved the establishment of a FIDE rating system for Fischer Random Chess (Chess960), with the condition that the rating system shall be elaborated and implemented no later than 1 June 2027. This responds to the continued growth of the variant and the need for an official competitive rating framework. The proposal was submitted jointly by the German Chess Federation, Icelandic Chess Federation, Norwegian Chess Federation, Irish Chess Union and Faroe Islands Chess Federation. The initiative noted that Chess960 has been growing internationally, while the absence of an official rating system has limited its integration into the wider competitive chess ecosystem.

FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030

The General Assembly noted the readiness of the Qatar Chess Association and the Georgia Chess Federation to host the FIDE Chess Olympiad 2030, together with the FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities 2030 and the FIDE Congress 2030. The Assembly instructed the FIDE Management Board to conduct negotiations with the Qatar Chess Association and, subject to the provision of official organisational and financial guarantees, to inform the FIDE Council and sign the respective contract following formal approval. Should the required official guarantees not be provided and the contract not be signed within a reasonable timeframe, the right to sign the contract will pass to the Georgia Chess Federation, subject to the provision of the corresponding organisational and financial guarantees.

Extraordinary General Assembly

The General Assembly decided that an Extraordinary General Assembly of FIDE will convene online in late 2026. The FIDE Council was instructed to prepare the FIDE budget for 2027 and the provisional FIDE budget for 2028, and submit them for review at the Extraordinary General Assembly.

The full list of decisions and the official documentation will be published at a later date .
